title: Make the character move
intro: Four steps, one script that grows. The robot stands on a stage 600 pixels wide. Each step adds a little to the same script, and the stage beside the editor runs whatever you have written so far.

steps.title: Put the robot on the stage
steps.prompt: The stage is a strip 600 pixels wide. The robot's place on it is a number: how many pixels from the left edge it stands. Declare a variable at the top of the script (a member variable) called `x` that starts at the number `0`, so the robot begins at the left edge, and another one called `speed` that starts at the number `120`. Nothing moves yet; this step only gives the robot its two numbers.
steps.starter:
# The robot stands on the stage at x, and will move at speed.
# Declare both member variables here.
hints: A member variable is declared at the top of the script, outside any function, with `var`.
`var x = 0` on one line and `var speed = 120` on the next is all this step needs.

docs.name: var
docs.what: declares a variable; at the top of a script it is a member variable that every function can use

steps.title: Move on command
steps.prompt: Now give the robot two commands. Write `move_right`, which takes one parameter, `distance`, and adds it to `x`. Then write `move_left`, which takes `distance` and takes it away from `x`. The buttons beside the stage call your functions with the number `40`; the checks call them with other numbers too.
steps.starter:
var x = 0
var speed = 120

# Write move_right(distance) and move_left(distance) below.

tests.name: move_left(20) from the start goes to -20

hints: A function with a parameter looks like `func move_right(distance):`, and its body is indented under it.
`x += distance` adds to a variable at the top of the script (a member variable); `-=` takes away.
Both functions change `x`, the same member variable from step 1. Neither needs `return`.

docs.name: func
docs.what: defines a function; a name in the brackets is a parameter, a value handed in with each call
adds to a variable in place; -= takes away

steps.title: Move every frame
steps.prompt: A game redraws the screen many times a second; each redraw is a frame. Godot calls `_process(delta)` once per frame, where `delta` is how long that frame took, in seconds, usually about 0.016. Write `_process` so that every frame it adds `speed * delta` to `x`. Over one second the small additions add up to exactly `speed` pixels, whatever the frame rate. The Play button beside the stage runs 60 frames for you.
steps.starter:
var x = 0
var speed = 120

func move_right(distance):
	x += distance

func move_left(distance):
	x -= distance

# Write _process(delta) below.

tests.name: One second of frames moves the robot by speed
Half a second moves it half as far
Fewer, longer frames cover the same distance
A command and the frames add together

hints: The function is `func _process(delta):`. Godot passes delta in; you never call _process yourself.
Each frame the robot should move `speed * delta` pixels, so add that to `x`.
If the robot jumps a whole `speed` every frame, the multiply by `delta` is missing.

docs.name: _process(delta)
docs.what: a function Godot calls every frame; delta is that frame's length in seconds

steps.title: Faster and slower
steps.prompt: Last, let the speed change while the robot runs. Write `speed_up`, which takes `amount` and adds it to `speed`, and `slow_down`, which takes `amount` and takes it away. Because `_process` reads `speed` every frame, the robot moves at the new speed from the next frame on. The buttons use the number `60`.

tests.name: A faster robot covers more ground in a second
At speed 0 the robot stands still

hints: These two are the same shape as move_right and move_left, but they change `speed` instead of `x`.

docs.what: adds to a variable in place; -= takes away

godot: Open Godot and make a new project called Robot Moves.
Create a 2D scene. Rename the root node to Robot.
Add a Sprite2D as a child of Robot and drag icon.svg from the FileSystem dock into its Texture.
Attach a script to Robot (the scroll icon above the scene tree). Keep the default name.
At the top of the script declare `var speed = 120`. In Godot the robot's place is the built-in `position`, so there is no `x` to declare.
Write `func _process(delta):` and inside it `position.x += speed * delta`.
Run the scene (F6). The icon slides to the right and off the screen.
Change speed to the number `240` and run again: twice as fast.
Write `func move_right(distance):` with `position.x += distance` in it. Call `move_right(200)` inside `func _ready():`, run, and the robot starts further along.
